name: Core: Network Access
description: 45 original questions for Network Access (20% of the v1.1 blueprint).
author: CCNA Academy

questions.stem: After 'switchport mode access', which command places interface Gi0/4 in VLAN 30?
questions.explanation: Access ports carry one untagged data VLAN set with 'switchport access vlan <id>'. If the VLAN does not exist, IOS typically creates it.
questions.whyCorrect: This assigns the access port's data VLAN.
whyWrong: This is not a valid IOS interface command.
'vlan 30' is a global command that creates the VLAN; it does not assign ports.
This sets the untagged VLAN on a trunk, not an access port's VLAN.

questions.stem: A PC on Gi0/11 is configured as 192.168.10.50/24 with gateway 192.168.10.1, the VLAN 10 gateway. It cannot reach anything. Based on the output, what is the cause?
questions.exhibit:
SW1# show vlan brief
VLAN Name        Status    Ports
---- ----------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default     active    Gi0/12
10   STAFF       active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4, Gi0/5
                           Gi0/6, Gi0/7, Gi0/8, Gi0/9, Gi0/10
20   GUEST       active    Gi0/11
questions.explanation: Always confirm the port's VLAN matches the host's subnet. Fix with 'switchport access vlan 10' on Gi0/11.
options: Gi0/11 is in VLAN 20 instead of VLAN 10
Gi0/11 is configured as a trunk port
The gateway must be in VLAN 1
questions.whyCorrect: The PC is addressed for VLAN 10 but connected to a VLAN 20 port, so it cannot reach its gateway.
whyWrong: Trunk ports do not appear in 'show vlan brief'; Gi0/11 is listed as an access port in VLAN 20.
VLAN 10 is listed as active.
Each VLAN uses its own gateway in its own subnet.

questions.stem: Which statements about VLAN 1 on a Cisco switch are true? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: VLAN 1 is the default and default native VLAN. Best practice is to move unused ports and the native VLAN away from VLAN 1.
options: All switch ports belong to VLAN 1 by default
VLAN 1 is in the extended VLAN range
Frames in VLAN 1 are always tagged on 802.1Q trunks
questions.whyCorrect: VLAN 1 is the default VLAN for every port. IOS does not allow removing the default VLAN.
whyWrong: The extended range is 1006–4094.
By default VLAN 1 is also the native VLAN, which is sent untagged.

questions.stem: An IP phone and a PC share Gi0/8, configured with 'switchport access vlan 10' and 'switchport voice vlan 20'. How is their traffic carried on the link to the switch?
questions.explanation: The voice VLAN lets one access port carry two VLANs: tagged voice (learned by the phone via CDP or LLDP) and untagged data.
options: Voice tagged VLAN 20; PC untagged VLAN 10
Both tagged with their own VLAN IDs
questions.whyCorrect: The phone tags voice traffic with the voice VLAN and passes the PC's untagged frames through.
whyWrong: Voice would then share the data VLAN, defeating the voice VLAN's purpose.
The PC sends normal untagged frames.
This reverses the roles.

questions.stem: True or false: Hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on the same switch can communicate directly without a router or Layer 3 switch.
questions.explanation: Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain and normally a separate subnet, so traffic between them must be routed.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is false. Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain and normally a separate subnet, so traffic between them must be routed.
whyWrong: The statement is false, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. PC1 sends a broadcast frame. Which devices receive it?
questions.explanation: A broadcast is flooded to all ports in the same VLAN, including across trunks that allow that VLAN. Other VLANs never see it.
questions.whyCorrect: Both are in VLAN 10; the broadcast crosses the trunk tagged with VLAN 10.
whyWrong: The PC behind the phone is also in VLAN 10 on SW1.
PC2 and PC4 are in VLAN 20, a different broadcast domain.
These are in VLAN 20 and never receive VLAN 10 broadcasts.

questions.stem: SW1 and SW2 are connected by an 802.1Q trunk, and both ends are configured with 'switchport trunk native vlan 99'. How do frames belonging to VLAN 99 cross the trunk?
questions.explanation: On an 802.1Q trunk, all VLANs are tagged except the native VLAN. Both ends must agree on the native VLAN.
options: They are dropped by the trunk
questions.whyCorrect: Native VLAN frames are sent without an 802.1Q tag.
whyWrong: Only non-native VLANs are tagged.
The native VLAN is carried untagged, not dropped.
The tag is never rewritten to VLAN 1.

questions.stem: SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1 are both configured with 'switchport mode dynamic auto'. What is the link's operational mode?
questions.explanation: DTP: desirable actively asks, auto only answers. auto + auto = access; desirable + auto/desirable/trunk = trunk.
options: Trunk carrying only the native VLAN
questions.whyCorrect: Dynamic auto only responds to trunk requests; neither side initiates, so no trunk forms.
whyWrong: A trunk needs at least one side set to trunk or dynamic desirable.
DTP disagreement does not err-disable the port.
There is no such DTP outcome.

questions.stem: After the configuration shown, an engineer enters 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 30' on Gi0/1. Which VLANs are allowed on the trunk?
questions.exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
questions.explanation: Use 'switchport trunk allowed vlan add <id>' to append, 'remove' to delete, and a bare list to replace.
questions.whyCorrect: Without the 'add' keyword, the command replaces the existing allowed list.
whyWrong: That result needs 'switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30'.
The new command overwrote the list.
The allowed list is restricted, not reset to all.

questions.stem: CDP reports a native VLAN mismatch: SW1 uses native VLAN 99 and SW2 uses native VLAN 1. What is the main risk?
questions.explanation: Configure the same native VLAN on both ends (ideally an unused VLAN) to prevent VLAN leakage and spanning-tree inconsistencies.
options: All VLANs stop being tagged on the trunk
Both switches automatically change their native VLAN to 1
questions.whyCorrect: Each side assigns untagged frames to its own native VLAN.
whyWrong: Tag size is always 4 bytes.
Non-native VLANs remain tagged.
Native VLANs are never adjusted automatically.

questions.stem: True or false: An 802.1Q tag adds 4 bytes to an Ethernet frame and contains a 12-bit VLAN ID.
questions.explanation: The tag carries TPID 0x8100 (16 bits), PCP (3 bits), DEI (1 bit) and the VLAN ID (12 bits), for 4 bytes total.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. The tag carries TPID 0x8100 (16 bits), PCP (3 bits), DEI (1 bit) and the VLAN ID (12 bits), for 4 bytes total.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Hosts in VLAN 10 can reach their gateway, but hosts in VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) cannot. Based on the configuration, what is wrong?
questions.exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
questions.explanation: In router-on-a-stick, each subinterface's 'encapsulation dot1Q <vlan>' must match the VLAN its hosts use, and the switch port must be a trunk.
options: Subinterface Gi0/0.20 uses 'encapsulation dot1Q 30' instead of 20
Routers need 'ip routing' to route between subinterfaces
The subinterface number must equal the VLAN ID
VLAN 20 must be the native VLAN
questions.whyCorrect: The router expects VLAN 30 tags on that subinterface, so VLAN 20 frames never reach it.
whyWrong: IPv4 routing is enabled by default on routers.
The number is only a label; the encapsulation VLAN is what matters.
Only one VLAN can be native, and it is not required here.

questions.stem: Which conditions are required for a Layer 3 switch to route between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 using SVIs? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: SVI routing: create VLANs, assign ports, configure 'interface vlan X' with an IP and 'no shutdown', and enable 'ip routing'.
options: Each SVI's VLAN exists and has at least one active port forwarding in it
A router-on-a-stick trunk to an external router
questions.whyCorrect: Without it, the switch does not route between its Layer 3 interfaces. An SVI is up/up only when its VLAN exists and has an active member port.
whyWrong: SVIs route internally; no external router is needed.
That command is used on router subinterfaces, not SVIs.

questions.stem: A router routes between VLANs using subinterfaces Gi0/0.10 (encapsulation dot1Q 10) and Gi0/0.20 (encapsulation dot1Q 20). How must the switch port connected to the router's Gi0/0 be configured?
questions.explanation: One physical router link carries multiple VLANs only when it is an 802.1Q trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN on the router.
options: As an access port in VLAN 10
questions.whyCorrect: The router's subinterfaces expect tagged frames for VLANs 10 and 20.
whyWrong: An access port would carry only VLAN 10.
A routed port carries no VLANs to the router's subinterfaces.
Link aggregation is unrelated to carrying multiple VLANs.

questions.stem: Which command shows the IP address and software version of a directly connected Cisco neighbor?
questions.explanation: CDP neighbor details are essential for documenting topology when diagrams are missing.
questions.whyCorrect: The detail view includes management addresses and the IOS version.
whyWrong: The summary view lists device ID, local and remote ports, capability and platform, but not IP addresses.
This shows CDP timers and status per interface.
This shows the local device's interfaces only.

questions.stem: A Cisco switch connects to a non-Cisco firewall. The engineer wants to see the firewall's system name and port from the switch. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Use LLDP in multi-vendor environments. Verify with 'show lldp neighbors [detail]'.
options: Configure the port as a trunk
questions.whyCorrect: LLDP is the vendor-neutral IEEE 802.1AB discovery protocol, often disabled by default on IOS.
whyWrong: CDP is Cisco proprietary and usually not supported by other vendors.
Trunking does not exchange device identity.
This shows a MAC address only, not system name or port.

questions.stem: Match each item to the correct value.
questions.explanation: CDP sends every 60 s with a 180 s holdtime. LLDP (802.1AB) sends every 30 s with a 120 s holdtime.
questions.whyCorrect: CDP default advertisement interval → 60 seconds; CDP default holdtime → 180 seconds; LLDP default advertisement interval → 30 seconds; LLDP standard → IEEE 802.1AB

questions.stem: SW1 and SW2 connect over two links. Both switches use 'channel-group 1 mode passive' on these ports. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Working combinations: active/active, active/passive (LACP), desirable/desirable, desirable/auto (PAgP), on/on (static).
questions.whyCorrect: Passive only responds to LACP; neither side starts negotiation.
whyWrong: LACP needs at least one side in active mode.
Passive is an LACP mode, not PAgP.
Static bundling uses mode on.

questions.stem: Which mode combinations successfully form an EtherChannel? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: At least one side must actively negotiate, and both sides must use the same protocol (or both use 'on').
options: active on one switch and passive on the other
desirable on one switch and auto on the other
on on one switch and active on the other
questions.whyCorrect: LACP active initiates and passive responds. PAgP desirable initiates and auto responds.
whyWrong: Neither side initiates LACP.
Neither side initiates PAgP.
Static 'on' does not negotiate, so it cannot pair with LACP.

questions.stem: Based on the output, what is the status of Gi0/2?
questions.exhibit:
SW1# show etherchannel summary
Flags:  D - down        P - bundled in port-channel
        I - stand-alone s - suspended
        H - Hot-standby (LACP only)
        R - Layer3      S - Layer2
        U - in use

Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi0/1(P)    Gi0/2(s)
questions.explanation: All EtherChannel members must match in speed, duplex, switchport mode and VLAN settings. Correct the mismatch and the port joins the bundle.
options: It is suspended due to a mismatch
It is bundled and forwarding traffic
It is a hot-standby LACP member
It is operating as a Layer 3 port
questions.whyCorrect: Flag (s) means suspended; common causes are VLAN, trunk or speed/duplex mismatches.
whyWrong: Bundled ports show flag (P), as Gi0/1 does.
Hot-standby ports show flag (H).
Layer 3 port-channels show flag R on the port-channel, and Po1 shows S (Layer 2).

questions.stem: True or false: EtherChannel load balancing is per flow, so one large file transfer between two hosts normally uses only one member link.
questions.explanation: A hash of addresses (and optionally ports) selects a member link per flow to keep packets in order. Many flows spread across links; a single flow does not.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. A hash of addresses (and optionally ports) selects a member link per flow to keep packets in order. Many flows spread across links; a single flow does not.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. Which switch is the root bridge for VLAN 10, and why?
questions.explanation: Bridge ID = priority (+ VLAN ID system-ID extension) + MAC. SW1's 24586 is lower than 32778, so SW1 is root regardless of MAC.
options: SW1, because it has the lowest bridge priority
SW3, because it has the highest MAC address
SW2, because it is connected to both other switches
No root is elected because priorities differ
questions.whyCorrect: The lowest bridge ID wins, and priority is compared before MAC address.
whyWrong: The lowest MAC is used only as a tiebreaker, and lowest wins.
Topology position does not determine the root.
Different priorities simply decide the election.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. Which port is in the alternate (discarding) role?
questions.explanation: Root ports point toward the root; each segment gets one designated port; remaining ports discard. Ties are broken by the lowest bridge ID.
questions.whyCorrect: On the SW2–SW3 segment, SW2 has the lower bridge ID and owns the designated port, leaving SW3's port as alternate.
whyWrong: SW2's port is designated on that segment.
All root bridge ports are designated.
That is SW3's root port (lowest cost to the root).

questions.stem: A non-root switch can reach the root through path A (one 100 Mbps link) or path B (two 1 Gbps links). Using default short path costs, which path is used for its root port?
questions.explanation: Default short costs: 10 Mbps = 100, 100 Mbps = 19, 1 Gbps = 4, 10 Gbps = 2. Root path cost is the sum along the path.
options: Path B, with a total cost of 8
Path A, with a total cost of 19
Both paths, because STP load-balances equal-cost paths
Path A, because it crosses fewer switches
questions.whyCorrect: Each 1 Gbps link costs 4, so 4 + 4 = 8, which is lower than 19.
whyWrong: 19 is higher than 8.
STP picks a single root port.
STP compares cost, not hop count.

questions.stem: Which command makes SW2 the root bridge for VLAN 20 by automatically setting a low enough priority?
questions.explanation: Use 'root primary' / 'root secondary', or set 'spanning-tree vlan X priority N' with N as a multiple of 4096.
questions.whyCorrect: This sets priority to 24576, or lower if needed, to win the election.
whyWrong: Priority must be a multiple of 4096, so IOS rejects 30000.
This is not valid IOS syntax.
Mode selects the STP variant (e.g., rapid-pvst), not the root.

questions.stem: Match each STP protection feature to its behavior.
questions.explanation: PortFast speeds up host ports; BPDU Guard protects them from switches; Root Guard protects root placement; Loop Guard protects against unidirectional-link loops.
questions.whyCorrect: PortFast → Moves an edge port immediately to forwarding; BPDU Guard → Err-disables an edge port that receives a BPDU; Root Guard → Blocks a port that receives superior BPDUs (root-inconsistent); Loop Guard → Stops a non-designated port from forwarding when BPDUs stop arriving
right: Moves an edge port immediately to forwarding
Err-disables an edge port that receives a BPDU
Blocks a port that receives superior BPDUs (root-inconsistent)
Stops a non-designated port from forwarding when BPDUs stop arriving

questions.stem: True or false: In Rapid PVST+, the port states are discarding, learning and forwarding.
questions.explanation: RSTP merges the legacy disabled, blocking and listening states into one discarding state.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. RSTP merges the legacy disabled, blocking and listening states into one discarding state.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: A user plugs a small managed switch into a wall port configured with PortFast and BPDU Guard. The port immediately becomes err-disabled. Why?
questions.explanation: BPDU Guard keeps unauthorized switches off edge ports. After removing the switch, recover with shutdown/no shutdown or errdisable recovery.
options: The port received a BPDU from the new switch
Port security detected a second MAC address
questions.whyCorrect: BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast port that receives any BPDU.
whyWrong: Port security is not mentioned and would report a security violation.
Duplex problems do not err-disable ports.
CDP does not disable ports.

questions.stem: Arrange the spanning-tree decision process in order.
questions.explanation: STP elects the root first, then root ports (best path to root), then designated ports per segment; everything else discards.
questions.whyCorrect: Elect the root bridge → Select one root port on each non-root switch → Select one designated port on each segment → Place all remaining ports in the alternate/blocking role
items: Select one root port on each non-root switch
Select one designated port on each segment
Place all remaining ports in the alternate/blocking role

questions.stem: Which AP mode lets a branch AP keep switching client traffic locally if the WAN link to the central WLC fails?
questions.explanation: FlexConnect is designed for branches across a WAN: control traffic goes to the WLC while client data can be switched locally.
questions.whyCorrect: FlexConnect APs can switch client data locally and keep serving clients without the WLC.
whyWrong: Local-mode APs tunnel all client traffic to the WLC and depend on it.
Monitor mode serves no clients.
Sniffer mode captures traffic for an analyzer and serves no clients.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. The APs operate in Local mode. Why are they connected to access ports rather than trunk ports?
questions.explanation: Local mode → access port (management VLAN). FlexConnect with local switching → trunk. WLC → trunk to reach many client VLANs.
options: Client traffic is tunneled to the WLC in CAPWAP
questions.whyCorrect: The WLC places client traffic into VLANs, not the access switch.
whyWrong: APs in FlexConnect mode use trunks when switching multiple VLANs locally.
CAPWAP uses any routable management VLAN.
PoE works on trunk ports too.

questions.stem: Which statements about CAPWAP are correct? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: CAPWAP builds tunnels between lightweight APs and the WLC: control (5246) and data (5247).
options: Encrypting the data channel is mandatory
questions.whyCorrect: CAPWAP control is carried on UDP 5246 and protected by DTLS. The data channel uses UDP 5247.
whyWrong: CAPWAP uses UDP.
Data-channel DTLS encryption is optional; control is always encrypted.

questions.stem: An AireOS WLC's distribution ports are bundled with LAG to a Catalyst switch. Which switch interface configuration is required?
questions.explanation: AireOS WLC LAG is static, so the switch side must be 'mode on', with matching trunk settings.
questions.whyCorrect: AireOS LAG does not negotiate, so the switch must use a static EtherChannel.
whyWrong: LACP negotiation is not supported by AireOS LAG.
PAgP is not supported by AireOS LAG.
Passive LACP waits for a peer that will never negotiate.

questions.stem: Match each AP mode to its purpose.
questions.explanation: Choose AP mode by purpose: Local for campus, FlexConnect for branches, Monitor for RF security/location, Sniffer for troubleshooting captures.
questions.whyCorrect: Local → Serves clients and tunnels all client traffic to the WLC; FlexConnect → Serves clients and can switch traffic locally at a branch; Monitor → Serves no clients; scans RF for rogues and location; Sniffer → Captures 802.11 frames and forwards them to a packet analyzer
right: Serves clients and tunnels all client traffic to the WLC
Serves clients and can switch traffic locally at a branch
Serves no clients; scans RF for rogues and location
Captures 802.11 frames and forwards them to a packet analyzer

questions.stem: In the WLC GUI, an administrator creates a WLAN dedicated to IP phones. Which QoS profile should be selected?
questions.explanation: WLC QoS profiles: Platinum (voice), Gold (video), Silver (best effort), Bronze (background).
questions.whyCorrect: Platinum is intended for voice.
whyWrong: Gold is intended for video.
Silver is best effort (the default).
Bronze is for background traffic.

questions.stem: Clients connect to the 'Corp' SSID but receive addresses from the guest subnet. Which WLAN setting is most likely misconfigured?
questions.explanation: On a WLC, each WLAN is mapped to an interface (VLAN). A wrong mapping puts clients in the wrong subnet.
questions.whyCorrect: This mapping decides which VLAN (and DHCP scope) clients join.
whyWrong: QoS affects prioritization, not addressing.
Broadcasting the SSID does not affect which subnet clients use.
Security controls authentication and encryption, not the client VLAN.

questions.stem: SSH connections to SW1 fail, although its management SVI is reachable. Based on the configuration, which step is missing?
questions.exhibit:
hostname SW1
ip domain-name lab.local
username admin secret Str0ngPass!
!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh
questions.explanation: SSH prerequisites: hostname, ip domain-name, RSA keys (≥768 bits for SSHv2), local user (or AAA), 'login local' and 'transport input ssh' on the VTY lines.
options: Generating RSA keys with 'crypto key generate rsa'
questions.whyCorrect: SSH stays disabled until RSA keys exist; hostname and domain name are already set.
whyWrong: Privileged EXEC access is not required to open an SSH session.
SSHv1 is obsolete and is not required.
This only obscures clear-text passwords in the config.

questions.stem: An engineer must copy an IOS image to a router across a network where credentials must not be sent in clear text. Which protocol is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For secure file transfer to network devices, use SCP or SFTP. TFTP and FTP are acceptable only on trusted management networks.
questions.whyCorrect: SCP runs over SSH, so both authentication and data transfer are encrypted.
whyWrong: TFTP has no authentication or encryption.
FTP authenticates, but credentials and data are sent in clear text.
Telnet is a remote CLI protocol, not file transfer, and is unencrypted.

questions.stem: True or false: Console access to a router works even if the router has no IP address configured.
questions.explanation: The console is an out-of-band serial connection that does not depend on IP, which is why it is used for initial setup and recovery.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. The console is an out-of-band serial connection that does not depend on IP, which is why it is used for initial setup and recovery.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which VLAN ID belongs to the extended VLAN range?
questions.explanation: Normal range: 1–1005 (1002–1005 reserved). Extended range: 1006–4094. VLAN IDs are 12 bits.
questions.whyCorrect: The extended range is 1006–4094.
whyWrong: 1000 is in the normal range (1–1005).
VLAN 1 is the default VLAN in the normal range.
1002–1005 are reserved normal-range VLANs.

questions.stem: Which command displays the native VLAN and the allowed VLANs of every trunk port?
questions.explanation: 'show interfaces trunk' is the first command to run when a VLAN does not cross a trunk.
questions.whyCorrect: It lists mode, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed, active and forwarding VLANs per trunk.
whyWrong: It lists access ports per VLAN and omits trunks.
It shows STP roles and states, not trunk allowed lists.
It shows neighbors, not trunk configuration.

questions.stem: Which VTY line configuration allows only SSH logins authenticated against local usernames?
questions.explanation: Combine local (or AAA) authentication with SSH-only transport, plus exec-timeout and an ACL with access-class for further hardening.
options: login local and transport input ssh
password cisco, login, transport input all
login local and transport input telnet ssh
no login and transport input ssh
questions.whyCorrect: 'login local' uses the local user database and 'transport input ssh' rejects Telnet.
whyWrong: This uses a shared line password and allows Telnet.
Telnet is still permitted.
'no login' disables authentication entirely.

questions.stem: In VLAN 1, SW1 has bridge priority 32769 and MAC 0011.1111.1111; SW2 has bridge priority 32769 and MAC 0011.1111.0001. Which switch is the root bridge?
questions.explanation: 32769 = 32768 default priority + VLAN 1 (system ID extension). Compare priority first, then MAC.
options: SW2, because the priorities tie and its MAC address is lower
SW1, because its MAC address is higher
Neither, because the priorities are identical
Both switches share the root bridge role
questions.whyCorrect: The MAC address breaks the tie, and lower wins.
whyWrong: STP prefers the lowest bridge ID.
A tie in priority is always resolved by the MAC address.
Each STP instance has exactly one root bridge.

questions.stem: Which items are required to build a Layer 3 EtherChannel between two multilayer switches? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Layer 3 EtherChannel members appear with flag R (Layer 3) in show etherchannel summary.
options: 'no switchport' on the member interfaces and the port-channel interface
The IP address configured on the port-channel interface
An IP address on each member interface
questions.whyCorrect: Layer 3 port-channels use routed ports. The logical interface carries the address, not the members.
whyWrong: Members carry no individual addresses.
Trunking is a Layer 2 concept.

questions.stem: 'show interfaces trunk' lists VLAN 30 under 'Vlans allowed on trunk' but not under 'Vlans allowed and active in management domain'. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Create the VLAN ('vlan 30') or make sure VTP is propagating it. The trunk output lists allowed, active and forwarding VLANs separately.
options: VLAN 30 has not been created on this switch
questions.whyCorrect: A VLAN must exist in the local VLAN database to be active on the trunk.
whyWrong: The native VLAN would still be active.
STP blocking is shown in the 'forwarding state and not pruned' list.
Encapsulation does not remove VLANs from the active list.
